Wetland weeds: They are tender annuals with semi-aquatic habit. They can thrive as well under water logged and in partially dry condition. Propagation is chiefly by seed. E.g., Eclipta alba (Bhringraj), Ammannia baccifera (Scarlet pimpernel).

Garden land weeds (Irrigated lands): These weeds neither require large quantities of water like wetland weeds nor can they successfully withstand extreme drought as dryland weeds. E.g., Trianthema portulacastrum (Santhi), Digera arvensis.
Dry lands weeds: These are usually hardy plants with deep root system. They are adapted to withstand drought on account of mucilaginous nature of the stem and hairiness. E.g., Argemone mexicana.
Weeds of black cotton soil: These are often closely allied to those that grow in dry condition. E.g., Aristolochia bracteate (worm killer).
Weeds of red soils: They are like the weeds of garden lands consisting of various classes of plants. E.g., Commelina benghalensis (Day flower).
Weeds of light, sandy or loamy soils: Weeds that occur in soils having good drainage. E.g., Leucas aspera (Thumbai).
Weeds of laterite soils: Lantana camara (grows in roadside), Spergula arvensis
Weeds of crop lands: The majority of weeds infests the cultivated lands and cause hindrance to the farmers for successful crop production. E.g., Phalaris minor in wheat
Weeds of pasture lands: Weeds found in pasture / grazing grounds. E.g., Indigofera enneaphylla
Weeds of waste places: Corners of fields, margins of channels etc., where weeds grow in profusion. E.g., Gynandropsis pentaphylla, Calotropis gigantean
Weeds of playgrounds, road-sides: They are usually hardy, prostrate perennials, capable of withstanding any amount of trampling. E.g., Alternanthera echinata, Tribulus terestris
6. Based on cotyledon number: Based on number of cotyledons it possess it can be classified as dicots and monocots.

Monocots: The seeds of the plant have one cotyledon, plants have fibrous root system, Leaves have parallel venation, Flower parts are present in multiples of 3.Also known as narrow leaf or grass weeds. Graminea is the most important family for monocotyledon weeds. E.g., Panicum flavidum, Echinochloacolona(Other plants: Wheat, corn, millet, lilies, sugarcane, banana, onion, ginger, palm, and bamboo)

Dicots: The seeds of the plant have two cotyledons, Plants mostly have tap root system, Leaves have reticulated venation, Flower parts are present in the multiple of 4 or 5. Also known as broadleaf weeds. Asteraceae is the most important family for Di-cotyledon weeds.E.g., Crotalaria verucosa, Indigofera viscose.(Other plants: Mango, Peanut, Pea, Tomato, Lettuce, Rose, Apple etc.)
7. Based on soil pH: Based on pH of the soil the weeds can be classified into three categories.
Acidophile: Acid soil weeds E.g., Rumex acetosella.
Basophile : Saline & alkaline soil weeds E.g., Taraxacum sp.
Neutrophile: Weeds of neutral soils eg Acalypha indica
8. Based on morphology: Based on the morphology of the plant, the weeds are also classified in to three categories. This is the most widely used classification by the weed scientists.
Grasses: All the weeds come under the family Poacee are called as grasses which are characteristically having long narrow spiny leaves. The examples are Echinocloa colonum Cynodon dactylon.

Sedges: The weeds belonging to the family Cyperaceae come under this group. The leaves are mostly from the base having modified stem with or without tubers. The examples are Cyperus rotundus, Fimbrystylis miliaceae.

Broad leaved weeds: This is the major group of weeds as all other family weeds come under this except that is discussed earlier. All dicotyledon weeds are broad leaved weeds. The examples are Flavaria australacica, Digera arvensis, Tridax procumbens.
9. Based on nature of stem: Based on development of bark tissues on their stems and branches, weeds are classified as woody, semi-woody and herbaceous species.
Woody weeds: Weeds include shrubs and under shrubs and are collectively called brush weeds. E.g., Lantana camera, Prosopis juliflora.
Semi-woody weeds: E.g.,Croton sparsiflorus
Herbaceous weeds: Weeds have green, succulent stems are of most common occurrence around us. E.g., Amaranthus viridis
Absolute weeds: Weeds are wild plants or weedy plants in nature and have no value as crops or any use to farmers under any circumstance, E.g., Polygonum sp. Rumex Spp.

Relative weeds: They are not weeds in nature, but because of their sudden occurrence, or relative presence with certain crop of prime importance, are treated as weed, in strict sense, relative to that situation only. Elsewhere, it may be growing as a crop or other purpose. Undesirable crop plants in the main crop field. For example:- mustard is a weed in wheat field, maize in sorghum field. :

Rogues: Few plants of a variety of a crop growing here and there in a scattered manner in another variety of prime importance and preferably grown for a situation are treated as rogues. Other variety plant in the same crop. For example:- HD 2329 wheat variety in HD 2285 wheat field and Alemaya Composite variety of maize in rare or Buktiri variety of maize are rogues.
Volunteer weeds: Such weeds are grown from the fallen seeds of previous or preceding crop in the field.
Note: A few weeds may produce seed through apomixis i.e without fertilization. E.g., Ferns reproduce by spores.

Parasitic weeds: The parasite weeds are either total or partial which means, the weeds that depend completely on the host plant are termed as total parasites while the weeds that partially depend on host plant for minerals and capable of preparing its food from the green leaves are called as partial parasites. Those parasites which attack roots are termed as root parasites and those which attack shoots of other plants are called as stem parasites. The typical examples are:
Total root parasite: Orabanche cernua (Broomrape) on Tobacco
Partial root parasite: Striga lutea (Witch weed) on sugarcane and sorghum
Total stem parasite: Cuscuta chinensis on lucerne and onion
Partial stem parasite: Loranthus longiflorus on mango and other trees

C. Aquatic weeds: Unwanted plants. which grow in water and complete at least a part of their life cycle in water are called as aquatic weeds. They are further grouped into four categories as submersed, emersed, marginal and floating weeds.
These weeds are mostly vascular plants that produce all or most of their vegetative growth beneath the water surface, having true roots, stems and leaves.
Example: BGA (Anabaena spp.), Pond weed (Potamogeton spp), Vallisnaria, Hydrilla spp.

These plants are rooted in the bottom mud, with aerial sterns and leaves at or above the water surface. The leaves are broad in many plants and sometimes like grasses. These leaves do not rise and fall with water level as in the case of floating weeds.
E.g., Nelumbium speciosum, Jussieua repens.
Most of these plants are emersed weeds that can grow in moist shoreline areas with a depth of 60 to 90 cm water. These weeds vary in size, shape and habitat.
The important genera that come under this group are; Typha, Polygonum, Cephalanthus, Scirpus etc.

These weeds have leaves that float on the water surface either singly or in cluster. Some weeds are free floating and some rooted at the mud bottom and the leaves rise and fall as the water level increases or decreases.
Example waterer hyacinth (Echhornia crassipes), water fern (Salvinia molesta), water lettuce (Pistia sp.), water velvet (Azola pinnata).
Rooted weeds with floating leaves: lotus (Nelumbo nucifera), white water lily (Nymphaea alba).
Emergent weeds /Semi-aquatic weeds: Grow in shallow water. Typha spp., Ipomoea sp., pickerel weed (Pontederia cordata).
Among all aquatic weeds the water hyacinth (E. crassipes) is the most troublesome aquatic weed.

blocks.text: Total root/holo-root parasite: They take away food from the host-roots and do not have any other source of gathering food. Therefore, they are also called obligate root-parasite.
For example, Orobanche spp. (Broomrape) on tobacco, tomato, fababean, chickpea, mustard, etc.

Partial root/hemi-root parasite: Initially they depend upon host-roots for their food and living (sub-terranean/under-ground stage in case of Striga), but later after emergence from soil, they are green, chlorophyllous and can produce their own food.
For example, Striga hermonthica/asiatica=lutea (Witch weed) on sorghum, maize, sugarcane and Striga generoides on cowpea.
Total stem/holo-stem parasite: They take away food from the host-shoot/stem and do not have any other source of gathering food. Therefore, they are also called obligate shoot/ stemparasite.

For example, Cuscuta campesstris/chinesis/epilinum on alfalfa (lucerne, Medicago sativa), niger and linseed, espectively. Earlier Cuscuta was the only parasitic genus of the autotrophic family Convolvulaceae. But now-a-days Cuscutaceae, a separate family has come into being for this genus.
Partial stem/hemi-stem parasite: Initially they depend upon the host-shoot/stem for their food, but later for becoming green and chlorophyllous, can produce their own food.

For example, Loranthus longiflorus is a green colour plant on mango and other trees and Cassytha filiformis on orange, eucalyptus and other trees. Cassytha filiformis has circumnutation anticlock-wise like Cuscuta but is much greener than Cuscuta.

blocks.text: Absolute weeds: These are always weeds. Plant of no economic importance for human being. E.g., Cyprus spp., Argemone mexicana, Bathua in wheat
Relative weeds: These are other crop plants. Undesirable crop plants in the main crop field E.g., barley in wheat.
Volunteer plants: Growing of plant in main crop due to seed shading from the previous sown crop.

Rogue weeds: Unwanted plant that grow profusely where it is not desired or any economical plant growing out of its proper place. E.g., Plants of C-306 variety grown in Raj- 4037 variety of wheat crop.
Roguing: Removal of off type plant from main crop.
Objectionable weeds: Weeds which produce seeds that are difficult to separate once mixed in crop seeds because of resemblance with crop seeds.
Crop specific weeds: Due to need for specific microclimate E.g., Chicory required cool and moist climate hence it grows well in berseem field.
Noxious weeds: Undesirable, troublesome and difficult to control. E.g., Cyprus spp., Cynodon dactylon, Parthenium sp., Lantana, Cuscuta, Orobanche, Eichornia, Salvinia, Sorghum helpense etc.
Mimicry weeds: These weeds are morphologically similar with main crop. E.g., Phalaris minor in wheat and Echinochloa spp. in rice.
Satellite weeds: Weeds mature at the same time and height along with crop and seeds are similar to main crop so difficult to separation of seeds from main crop. E.g., Avena fatua in Barley
Dispersal of weed seeds from mother plant to another place. It includes several mechanisms:
Autochory: Exercised by weed plant themselves with special structure i.e., pappus, wing, baloon, persistent style, comose, It's dominant in legume seeds.
Allochory: Seeds are dispersed by extraneous factors/agents i.e., human, animal, birds, water, wind, crop seed, FYM etc.
Anemochory: weed seeds dispersal by wind: following type structure performs of transportation. (Trick: PCB PCP)
Pappus: a parachute like modification of calyx in to hairs E.g., Tridar procumbens.
Comose: some seeds of weeds are covered with hairs e.g., Calotropis sp.
Balloon: calyx modified that enclosed the seeds loosely along with entrapped air E.g., Physalis minima
Myrmecochory: weed seed dispersal by ants (insects) is known as Myrmecochory.
Autochory: self-dispersal mechanisms of weed seeds is known as Autochory
Zoochory: animals mediated dispersal
Endozoochory: viability of weed seeds in animal excreta after digestion is referred as Endozoochory
Epizoochory: dispersal by adhesion of seeds on out-side of animals is known as Epizoochory
Anthropochory: human mediated dispersal (special kind of zoochory), it is main cause of biological invasion.
Innate/inherent (Primary dormancy): Due to genetic factors and chemical inhibitors in seed coat.
Induced (Secondary dormancy): Dormancy due to environmental factors (Temperature/water logging)
Enforced: Dormancy in this case enforced (deep placement) & by unfavourable condition.
Wild oat (Avena fatua) exhibited all three types of dormancies (Reported by Thurston 1959)
Quiescence: Resting condition of seed (a type of dormancy). Due to unfavourable conditions.

rows: Genetically controlled dormancy, (Failed to germinate even if they were present in the top 3 to 5 cm soil)
Due to sudden physio changes like water logging, rise in soil temperature, increased CO2 content of the soil, low O2 pressure

blocks.text: Weed control and weed management are the two terms used in weed science.
Weed control: It is the process of limiting infestation of the weed plant so that crops can be grown profitably.

Weed management: It includes prevention, eradication and control by regulated use, restricting invasion, suppression of growth, prevention of seed production and complete destruction. Thus, weed control is one of the aspects of weed management.
Prevention, which means stopping a given weed species from contaminating an area, is often the most practical means of controlling weeds.
Eradication is the complete elimination of all living plants, including their vegetative propagules and seeds. Eradication is much more difficult than prevention or control.
It is an ideal weed control but rarely achieved

Control is the process of limiting weed infestations. In crops, the weeds are limited so that they have minimal effect on crop growth and yield. The degree of control is usually a matter of economics, a balance between the costs involved and the increase in profits due to the control of the weeds and the types of production systems and tools being used.

Weed control aims at only putting down the weeds present by some kind of physical or chemical means while weed management is a system approach whereby whole land use planning is done in advance to minimize the very invasion of weeds in aggressive forms and give crop plants a strongly competitive advantage over the weeds.
Sowing of weed free seeds.
Use of clean implements.
Removal of weed along the canal and irrigation channel.
Care in transplanting of seedling/plantlets.
Avoiding passing of cattle from weed infested area.
Crop management practices.
Enforcement of Weed Laws.
Quarantine methods and use of pre-emergence herbicides.
Blind Tillage: The tillage of the soil after sowing a crop before the crop plants emerge is known as blind tillage (In Sugarcane: 1 week after planting).
A stale seedbed is one where initial one or two flushes of weeds are destroyed before planting of a crop.
This is achieved by soaking a well-prepared field with either irrigation or rain and allowing the weeds to germinate.
The field is left as such for about one or two weeks.
Sufficient soil moisture particularly at the upper 3-5 cm layer/stratum will result in weed seed germination.

Control the emerged weeds by a non-residual herbicide, E.g., paraquat, glyphosate. glufosinate-ammonium (Aluminium sulphate used in tea nursery to lower soil pH ), or by shallow cultivation with spike -tooth harrow, spring -tooth harrow etc. Thus, the germination of initial 2 or more flushes of weeds are facilitated/ pampered/induced and later destroyed
Thereafter plant the crop with minimum soil disturbance to avoid exposing new weed seed, in favourable germination conditions.
Hand Pulling or Hand Weeding: Oldest method, Effective against annual weeds
Hand Hoeing: Effective against annual weeds, sowing in rows is pre-requisite.
Tillage: Shallow tillage for annual weeds, Deep tillage for perennial weeds.
Mowing and Sickling: Mowing under non-cropped areas while Slashing followed for both cropped and non-cropped, This method is useful for tall annual weeds.
Cono weeder, Dry Land weeder, Power rotary weeder, Tractor drawn weeding cum earthing up equipment

Sickling is also done by hand with the help of sickle to remove the top growth of weeds to prevent seed production and to starve the underground parts. It is popular in sloppy areas where only the tall weed growth is sickled leaving the root system to hold the soil in place to prevent soil erosion. Mowing is a machine-operated practice mostly done on roadsides and in lawns.
Chaining and dredging are obsolete control measures for aquatic weeds.

Chaining means pulling a heavy chain through the bottom of a ditch by two tractors moving on either bank of the ditch. The heavy chain, by its rubbing action cuts and up-roots the aquatic weeds, which later floats on the surface and gets collected down the stream by nets and hooks.
Dredging, on the contrary, is the mechanical pulling of weeds along with their shallow roots and rhizomes covered in mud. It is adopted to remove submerged and emerged aquatic weeds.
Cheeling simply means cutting and scraping of the top growth of weeds by the cheel hoe at the soil surfaces.
Digging in small scale may be carried out to remove the under-ground vegetative structures from the deeper layer of soil if found perennial weeds really problematic in certain area.
Herbicide: It derieved from Latin word, Herba (plant) and Caedre (to kill), means chemicals that kills or suppress the unwanted vegetations.
Weedicide: it was restricted term, chemicals that kills the weeds only
Before 1940, the era of inorganic herbicides like ashes, salts, copper sulphate, sodium arsenate, sodium nitrate, sodium chloride etc.
Era of organic herbicides was started with the discovery of 2, 4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2, 4-D) in 1940 (used as plant hormone).
Hammer and Turkey (1944) firstly observed that 2, 4-D successful controlled weeds in cereal crops.
2,4 -D is the first selective organic herbicide used in the World.
Revolution in weed control by discovery of 2,4-D (Pokorny, 1944) In India 2, 4-D first tested as herbicide in 1946 and introduced at commercially in filed level in 1948.
Herbicides are registered in India under the Insecticides Act, 1968.
[Destructive Insects and Pests Act (DIPA) of 1914]
In India, the Central Insecticide Board and Registration Committee (CIBRC) regulates and manages the use of herbicides and insecticides.
The major crops where maximum herbicides are used are rice, wheat and plantation crops.
The state where highest herbicides are used is Punjab followed by Andhra Pradesh and U.P.
The mostly used herbicides in India are Isoproturon (Replaced by Sulphosulfuron), butachlor, 2, 4 -D, glyphosate and atrazine.

Bioremediation: some weeds remove or accumulate heavy metals from soil or aquatic systems. E.g., Echhornia crassipes (Water hycinth) and Hydrilla serve for bioremediation of Lead, Mercury, and Cadmium.
Itai-itai disease is due to cadmium poisoning.
Methemoglobinemia is also called “blue baby syndrome”. This happens when there is not enough oxygen in the blood. It is due to high concentration of nitrate (NO3) in drinking water

Pre emergence: Application of herbicide 1-2 days after sowing or immediately after sowing of a crop but before the emergence of crop.

Selective herbicide: Herbicide which kills selectively a particular group of weeds in a mixed stand of plants. Examples: all the pre-emergence and post emergence applied herbicides of field crops, Propanil.

Non selective herbicide: Herbicide which kills any species of plant irrespective of weeds and crop. They are used in controlling weed in road sides and non-cropped area. Examples: paraquat, diquat, glyphosate, glufosinate, acrolein, picroram, amitrol etc.

blocks.text: Narrow spectrum herbicide: Herbicide which control particular group of weeds and due to their narrow range usually do not control even all the weeds of particular group. Example: 2, 4 D (kills only broad-leaved weeds and sedges, not grasses), metsulfuron-methyl etc.
Broad spectrum herbicide: Herbicide which control wide range of weeds (grasses, broadleaves, sedges). Example: atrazine, pendimethalin, imezathypr, alachlor, butachlor

Soil applied/ soil active herbicides: Applied to soil or active through soil and kill germinative weeds and their parts. E.g., all pre plant incorporation and pre-emergence herbicides are included in this category.

Foliage applied: Applied to foliage of plant or non-cropped weeds. E.g., all post emergence herbicides (2, 4-D, isoproturon, sulfosulfuron, metribuzin etc.) + non cropped herbicides (paraquat, glyphosate etc.).
Both soil and foliage active herbicides: atrazine, metribuzin have both actions.

blocks.text: Non residual / Zero persistence herbicide: these herbicides easily degraded or metabolized after application and leaves no or less residues in applied soil. E.g., Paraquat, diquat, glyphosate these are used zero/minimum tillage).

Residual herbicide: Herbicide which are more resistant 1o degradation and maintain their effect in soil for a considerable period of time after application e.g., 2, 4-D (3-4 week) Triazines (1-2 Year), Fenec (> 2 Years)

blocks.text: Temporary soil sterilants / fumigants: Herbicide which are basically fumigants and sterilize the soil for a relatively short period (Usually 15-16 weeks) E.g., methyl-bromide, metham etc.
Permanent soil sterilants: They remain active in soil for a relatively long period E.g., Triazines & Phenyl ureas.
Contact herbicide: These herbicides are being less mobility, kills the plant primarily by contact with the plant tissue E.g., paraquat, diquat, propanil, oxyfluorfen etc.

Systemic or translocated herbicides: Herbicide moves within the plant from the point of treatment to its other part to variable extent e.g., all herbicide except contact is systemic in nature like 2, 4-D, atrazine, pendimethalin, glyphosate, metribuzin etc.
Atrazine is systemic and contact herbicide.

In India herbicide resistance was first reported in wheat crop in Haryana where some biotype of Phalaris minor found resistance to Isoproturon (reported by Malik and Singh, 1993). Highest number of weeds found resistance against atrazine herbicide (66 weed species) and maximum number of weeds resistance has been reported in wheat crop.
Cross resistance: In this a weed biotype is resistance to two or more herbicide due to presence of single resistance mechanism.
Multiple resistances: In this a weed biotype is resistance to one herbicide due to the presence of two or more distinct resistance mechanism.

blocks.text: Soil active herbicides are applied uniformly on the surface of the soil either by spraying or by broadcasting. The applied herbicides are either left undisturbed or incorporated in to the soil. Incorporation is done to prevent the volatilization and photo-decomposition of the herbicides.

It is the application of herbicides in a concentrated band, about 7-10 cm below the soil surface for controlling perennial weeds. For this special type of nozzles introduced below the soil under the cover of a sweep hood.
E.g., Carbamate herbicides to control Cyperus rotundus, Nitralin herbicides to control Convolvulus arvensis

Application to a restricted band along the crop rows leaving an untreated band in the inter-rows. Later inter-rows are cultivated to remove the weeds. Saving in cost is possible here. For example, when a 30 cm wide band of a herbicide applied over a crop row that were spaced 90 cm apart, then two-third cost is saved.

Application of volatile chemicals in to confined spaces or in to the soil to produce gas that will destroy weed seeds is called fumigation. Herbicides used for fumigation are called as fumigants. These are good for killing perennial weeds and as well for eliminating weed seeds. e.g., Methyl bromide, Metham

It is the application of herbicides with irrigation water both by surface and sprinkler systems. In India farmers apply fluchloralin for chillies and tomato, while in western countries application of EPTC with sprinkler irrigation water is very common in Lucerne.

It is the uniform application of herbicides to standing crops without considering the location of the crop. Only highly selective herbicides are used here e.g., Spraying 2,4-Ethyl Ester to rice three weeks after transplanting.
It is the application of herbicides on weeds in between rows of crops by directing the spray only on weeds avoiding the crop. This could be possible by use of protective shield or hood.
For example, spraying of glyphosate in between rows of tapioca using hood to control Cyperus rotundus.

It is a method of applying non-selective herbicides on weeds by covering the crops which are wide spaced with polyethylene covers etc. This is expensive and laborious. However, farmers are using this technique for spraying glyphosate to control weeds in jasmine, cassava, banana.
It is usually done on small areas having serious weed infestation to kill it and to prevent its spread. Rope wick applicator and Herbicide glove are useful here.

IWM is a method whereby all economically, ecologically and toxicologically justifiable method are employed to keep the harmful organisms below the threshold level of economic damage, keeping in the foreground the conscious employment of natural limiting factors.
It is an environment friendly weed control approach.
Integrated Weed Management (IWM) approach aims at minimizing the residue problem in plant, soil, air and water.
An IWM involves the utilization of a combination of mechanical, chemical and cultural practices of weed management in a planned sequence, so designed as not to affect the ecosystem.

blocks.text: Allelopathy is a biological phenomenon by which an organism produces one or more biochemicals that influence the growth, survival, and reproduction of other organisms. These biochemicals are known as allelochemicals and can have beneficial (positive allelopathy) or detrimental (negative allelopathy) effects on the target organisms.
Allelopathy does not form any aspect of crop-weed competition, rather, it causes crop-Weed interference, it includes competition as well as possible allelopathy.
True Allelopathy: The direct or indirect harmful effect on the other crops through the release of toxic substance as such from the plant.
Functional Allelopathy: When precursor is released, which is converted into active substances by some microorganismis, is categorized under functional allelopathy.

Allelo chemicals are produced by plants as end products, by-products and metabolites liberalised from the plants; they belong to phenolic acids, flavanoides, and other aromatic compounds viz., terpenoids (Diterpenoid: GA3), steroids, alkaloids and organic cyanides. These chemicals are secondary metabolites and generally not required for metabolism (i.e., growth, development and reproduction) of the allelopathic organism.

Temporal Annidation (Annidation in Time): The complimentary interaction between the intercrops in the time aspect is called Temporal Annidation. Such intercrops have different natural habit and zero competition. Both the component species have widely varying duration and different peak demands for light and nutrients.

blocks.text: 1. Weed infestation: It refers to the percentage of weeds in the composite population of weed and crop plants.
(Total number of weeds in a unit area / Total no. of weed and crop plants in the same area) x 100
2. Weed Index or weed competition index: It refers to the reduction/gain in crop yield due to the presence of weeds in comparison to weed-free plots.
Lesser the weed index; better is the efficiency of herbicides and vice versa.
[(Yield from weed free (hand weeded) plots - yield from treated plots) / Yield from weed free (hand weeded) plots] x 100
3. Weed Control Efficiency (WCE): It indicates the percentage reduction in weed population or this weight of weeds under treated plot (herbicide) in comparison to untreated plot (weedy).
[(Weed count in unweeded plots - Weed count in treated plots) / Weed count in umweeded plots] x 100
4. Weed Smothering Efficiency (WSE): This index is used to determine the effect of intercropping on suppression of weeds in comparison to sole crop stand. (Asked in RRB SO-2020)
[(Weed dry weight in sole crop stand plots - Weed dry weight in intercropped plots) / Dry matter of weeds in sole crop stand Plots] x 100

blocks.text: Adjuvant: Chemicals employed to improve the herbicidal effects without being phytotoxic by themselves are called adjutants.

Safeners: Herbicide safeners are chemical compounds used in combination with herbicides to make them "safer" - that is, to reduce the effect of the herbicide on crop plants, and to improve selectivity between crop plants vs. weed species being targeted by the herbicide.
Emulsifiers: It allows petroleum-based pesticides (ECs) to mix with water.
Invert emulsifiers: It allows water-based pesticides to mix with petroleum carrier.
Thickeners: It reduces drift by increasing droplet size and reducing volume of spray contained in drift-prone droplets.
Buffers: It allows mixing of pesticides of different acidity or alkalinity.
Surfactants: are substances that absorb to surfaces or interfaces, causing a marked decrease in the surface tension.
Band application of herbicides: Application of herbicides in restricted area along the crop rows is called band application of herbicides.
Blanket application of herbicide: Uniform application of herbicides to standing crops with disregard to the location of the crop plants is called blanket application.
Epinasty: Increase growth on the upper surface of a plant organ or part causing it to bend downwards is called epinasty.
Flamming: Momentary exposure of green weeds to as high as 1000C temperature from flame throwers resulting in coagulating their cell protoplasm is called flaming.
Humicant: Chemicals which prevent rapid drying of herbicide sprays on the foliage thus providing an extended opportunity of herbicide absorption is called humicant.
Mowing: Cutting of a uniform growth of weeds from an entire area at ground level is called mowing.
Neutrophiles: Weeds that grow well in neutral soils are called neutrophiles.
Offset: Runners of floating weeds are called offsets.
Stolon: A runner instead of trailing on the soil surface, rises in the form of an arc before hitting the soil surface is called stolon.
Additive Response: Additive response is the total effect of a combination which is equal to the sum of the effects of the two components taken independently.

Synergistic Response: In synergistic response, the total effect of a combination is greater of more prolonged than the sum of the effects of the two taken independently. The mixture of 2,4-D and Chlorpropham is synergistic on monocot species generally resistant to 2,4-D.

Antagonistic Response: In antagonistic response, the total effect of a combination is smaller than the most active component applied alone. e.g., Combination of EPTC with 2,4-D, 2,4,5-T or dicamba have antagonistic responses in sorghum and giant foxtail.
Independent effect: The total effect of a combination is equal to the effect of the most active component applied alone.

Enhancement effect: The effect of an herbicide and non-toxic adjuvant applied in combination on a plant is said to have an enhancement effect if the response is greater than that obtained when the herbicide is used at the same rates without the adjuvant e.g., Mixing Ammonium sulphate with Glyphosate.

Radicle comes out from the seed coat in the form of soft structure and it moves towards the soil. It develops and shapes primary root.

Primary root: It is formed as a direct elongation of the radicle in most dicotyledonous plants. It grows inside the soil. It bears lateral roots of several orders like secondary, tertiary, etc. roots.

Lateral roots: They extend horizontally from the primary root (radicle) and serve to anchor the plant securely into the soil. The lateral roots help in uptake of water and nutrients required for the growth and development of the plant.
The primary root is large, central, and dominant root in taproot system. From the primary root other roots sprout laterally.
This root system is generally tapering in shape and grows directly downward. It is common in dicot plants.
It consists of thin, moderately branching roots growing from the base of the stem. The primary root is not prominent and is replaced by a large number of roots.
The fibrous root systems appear as a thick tuft of roots forming a mat-like structure at maturity. It is universal in monocotyledonous plants and ferns.
A root that arises from any point on the plant other than the radicle or the root axis.

Adventitious roots are plant roots that form from any non-root tissue and are produced both during normal development [crown roots on cereals and nodal roots on strawberry (Fragaria spp.)] and in response to stress conditions, such as flooding, nutrient deprivation, and wounding.

These roots are mainly involved in absorption of water and minerals from the soil, providing additional anchorage to the plant parts, storage of reserve food material and synthesis of plant growth hormones.
Example: Prop roots of banyan, corn, aerial roots of Monstera, willow (Salix) etc.

Roots of some plants modify their shape and structure to adapt for additional functions. Rather than absorption and conduction of water they perform additional functions like support, storage of food and respiration.
The primary tap roots are modified for storage of reserve food materials. The secondary roots remain thin. They absorb water and minerals.
The storage roots swell up and assume various forms such as
Conical: Carrot
Fusiform or spindle shape: Radish
Napiform or spherical: Turnip, beet
Tuberous: 4 o'clock plant
The plants which grow in marshy areas develop branches of root that come out of the ground and grow vertically upward.
This occurs as there is scarcity of oxygen in such places.
These roots are called pneumatophores.
Through these roots air moves inside the plant and cells get oxygen for cellular respiration.
Roots that arise from the higher nodes or branches of stem of certain plants to provide extra support.
Such stems are usually tall and slender and the prop roots develop at successively higher levels as the stem elongates. This is seen in banyan.
Adventitious root modified for storage: They are swollen and take up various shapes to accommodate the stored and reserve food like tuberous, fibrous, nodulous, beaded, etc.
Supporting roots that arise from lower nodes of the stem that are used to provide additional support.

These are adventitious roots that generally don't enter the soil and may absorb water and minerals from the air or from run-off from plants. These roots are found in the monocot families such as Araceae and Orchidaceae.
Example: Ficus glomerata (cluster fig tree, Indian fig tree or goolar (gular) fig), Epiphytic orchids
Contractile roots: These are roots which function to pull rootstock further into the soil. These are found in plant species with bulbs and corms.
Buttress roots: These are enlarged, horizontally spreading, and often vertically thickened roots at the base of trees that aid in mechanical support.
Climbing roots: Roots arise from nodes that help weak stemmed plants in climbing up with help of support as in the case of money plant.
Foliar roots: Roots arising from leaves as in case of Bryophyllum.
Seen in parasitic plants. These roots pierce through the host tissue a suck out the nutrients as in Cuscuta.
Example: Mistletoe (Viscum album) and Dodder (Cuscuta).

Prop roots are aerial roots that provide support to the tree. For example - banyan tree. Stilt roots are the roots that arise from the base of the plant and perform the function of supporting the plant. For example- sugarcane, maize.

After proper selection of site, nursery is laid out with the following nursery components such as fence, office room, store room, water source, mist tent, plant house, nursery yard, working space, waste pit, foot path, road and entrance.

An area of 0.25 ha has been considered for a viable nursery wherein 1.25 lakh seedlings can be raised. The size of the nursery may be increased according to the capacity and demand for planting material.

Forest classification is defined as the grouping and arrangement afforests based on defined criteria such as composition, age, climatic elements, structure, habitat, etc. As like any classification, forest classification is also based on many basic elements of forest or characteristics. This includes physiognomy, habitat, species composition, structure of forest, physiography, etc. The objectives and different schemes of forest classification are described here under.
To study and characterize the different forest types
To develop suitable silvicultural management techniques for different forests
To avoid wastage of resource and save money by avoiding failure
Even-aged forest or regular forest: Is a forest composed of even aged woods. A difference up to 25% is permitted in case of rotation is more than 100 years.

Uneven aged forest or irregular forest: Refers to the forest which is composed of trees of different ages. The age variation should be more than 25% of the rotation in case of long rotation or 20% of rotation for short rotation.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Forest classification based on growing stock
aliases: Forest classification based on growing stock

blocks.text: Normal forest: Is a forest which has a normal age gradation, growing stock and increment. It will give sustained yield and most ideal one. No virgin forests are normal forests.
Abnormal forest: Is a forest which do not have a normal age gradation, growing stock and increment. It gives irregular yield and not ideal one.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Forest classification based on species composition
aliases: Forest classification based on species composition

blocks.text: Pure forest: Is a forest which is mostly composed of one single species. The proportion of main species should not be less than 80 percent.
Mixed forest: Is a forest which is composed of two or more species in a storey. At least the canopy of one species must be more than 20%.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Forest types of India (Champion and Seth classification-1935)
aliases: Forest types of India (Champion and Seth classification-1935)

blocks.text: According to this system of classification, forests in India are classified in to five major groups.
These major groups are further divided in to sixteen groups based on climatic data and vegetation.

Group is further subdivided in to 2 or 3 sub groups viz., Andaman, southern or northern. Sub groups are classified in to types based on climax vegetation and series which are finally divided as subtypes. E.g., 1A - Southern tropical wet evergreen forests.
Regeneration is the renewal of forest crops by natural or artificial means. It may be either natural or artificial regeneration.

In a forest, competition among plants can be increased with increasing age. In order to obtain maximum yield the competition among the plants can be optimally managed by reducing the number of stems per unit area with the progress of age. All these can be covered under the tending operations.

Tending is defined as an operation carried out for the benefit of a forest crop at any stage of its life between the seedling and the mature stages. This includes weeding, cleaning, thinning, improvement felling, pruning, climber cutting and girdling.
This does not include regeneration felling, soil working, drainage, irrigation and controlled burning.
Tending helps in producing higher quality timber and thus by maximizes income. Tending differs from the cultural operation.

This is the most common method of planting. The number of plants per hectare of planting and spacing of plants is calculated as follows:

In simple terms clear felling is the removal of all trees from an area chosen for harvesting,
It is a silvicultural system in which equal or equiproductive areas of mature crops are successively clear felled in single operation. This is to be regenerated by either artificial or natural means.

It is a silvicultural system in which felling is done in the form of strips which progress successively in one direction across the area usually against the direction of wind. This is also referred as progressive clear felling strip system or progressive strip system.
Applicable: Pinus keysia.
To regenerate the area naturally by seed from the adjoining area
To protect the young crop against wind, snow, insects, fungal attack, etc.
It is a silvicultural system in which clear felling is done in the form of strips where the clear-felled strip is alternated with unfelled strips of similar width.
Applicable: Sal, Fir, Acacia mearnsii.
Crops obtained: Even aged

Uniform system is a kind of shelterwood system aiming at concentrated regeneration in which the canopy is uniformly opened up over the whole area of a compartment to obtain uniform regeneration. This is also referred as compartment system or shelterwood compartment system.
To provide shelter against adverse climatic factors
To regulate the light condition inside the forest for better regeneration
Applicable: Chir, deodar, kail

Consider a crop having a 100-year rotation. The regeneration period required for this crop is 25 years. Here the total area is divided in to four periodic blocks as it needs 25 years for its establishments. At a time, one PB is felled and regenerated with in the regeneration period Le., 25 years. Hence, instead of age gradation, this system creates age classes. This process is given in the following figure.

It is a silvicultural system in which regeneration felling are carried out in a scattered groups due to the presence of advance growth which induces regeneration de novo. This is also known as Bavarian femelschlag.
Applicable: Deodar and Khail
Group of promising advance growth is identified and located in the compartment.
Seeding felling is done all around the periphery (group I)
If advance growth is inadequate, gaps are created by felling.
Gap created will be more for light demanding species and vice versa.
Secondary felling is done when regeneration appears in gaps in the first group.
Now seeding felling is done around this (group II).
When regeneration comes up well in this, secondary felling is done in group II.
Now final felling is done in the group I and seeding felling is done in the successive areas (group III).
In this way, the felling proceeded so as to complete the whole forests.
Tending operations includes slash disposal, weeding, cleaning and shrub cutting.
Crop obtained: Younger crop is un-even aged, but it become even-aged at the end of rotation.

The shelterwood strip system is a silvicultural system in which regeneration felling are done, in the form of strips arranged successively from one side of the compartment to other usually against the direction of wind. The main objective is to get the protection against the wind.

It is a silvicultural system in which regeneration felling are carried out in narrow strips extending in east west direction and advancing from north to south direction. It provides the sideward protection to the regeneration from the sun. Hence, this system is useful for subtropical and tundra regions.

In this system, the pattern of felling is not prescribed and it may vary according to the local conditions. First clear felling is done in the northern side. Usually felling carried out from east to west direction.
The strip width should be half the height of standing trees. The secondary and final felling is similar to the shelterwood strip system.

Crop obtained is even aged along the east west direction whereas uneven aged crop in the north to south direction. It gives sloping profile to the canopy. As sun lie directly overhead, this system is not applicable under tropical conditions.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: e) The strip and group system
aliases: e) The strip and group system

blocks.text: It is a silvicultural system in which felling is done in strips conform to the group system. Here first seeding felling is done in an area where advance growth is presence. When regeneration comes up well, secondary felling carried out in the groups.

Simultaneously, adjacent strip is taken where seeding felling is started. Similarly work progressed till groups merges with each other. The direction of progress of strips should be against the direction of wind.

It is a silvicultural system in which the felling strip is located in the middle of the cutting section. The length of cutting section should be along the direction of wind. The strips are 2-5 m wide at a interval of 80 m. First initial seeding felling is made in this strip.

When regeneration comes up, it is widened more towards the leeward side and less towards the windward side. This gives a wedge shape to strips. With time progress, base of the strip touches each other as well as one end reaches the top end of the cutting section. Thereafter remaining areas in the strips are felled and regenerated. This system is suitable for wind prone area but the executing of works is more complicated one.

It is a silvicultural system in which regeneration felling are done in the pattern of group system but the regeneration period is long which resulting in irregular crop. This is also referred as Swiss femelschlag or Beden femelschlag. It is a compromise between selection system and shelter wood group system. This system is applicable to tropical rain forests.

It is a silvicultural system in which crop to be regenerated is opened up irregularly and the resultant crop is uneven aged. Regeneration is obtained naturally through irregular opening. This is applicable under the following conditions:
To reduce the unnecessary sacrifice of immature stand
In certain circumstance, regeneration is not obtained at our will
Area where there is a danger of loss of fertility
Crop obtained: Irregular crop.
It is a silvicultural system in which felling and regeneration are distributed over the whole area and the resultant crop is uneven aged. It differs from other systems in the following ways:
Regeneration felling is distributed over the whole area
In this system trees are felled in groups instead of being a scattered single tree.
The size of the group depends on the light requirement. This varies with aspect, slope, height of surrounding trees, etc.
In this, groups are not enlarged centrifugally, as like in shelterwood group system.
In small area whole area is carried out whereas in case of vast forest area, felling cycle is adopted.
Crop obtained is irregular. But within the groups, all trees are similar in age.
This is suitable for light demanders.
Applicable: Sal, teak, fir and spruce forests.

Accessory systems are those high forest systems which originates from other even aged systems through slight modifications. This is resulting in an irregular Or two storeyed high forests. The different types of this system, are as follows;
It is an accessory silvicultural system that results in the formation of a two storeyed forest.
Here the tree canopy occurs in two strata v/z., upper and lower canopy.
The dominant species in each stratum is different.
The crop in each storey is even aged.
The top canopy is of seedling origin.
Lower storey is obtained from natural regeneration but under planting is also done in the following circumstance.
It is essential for protection of soil. Cover crops used for these purposes are Mesua, Switenia, Evodia and Bamboo.
It is done to improve the proportion of valuable species inside the forest.
It helps propagation of certain species which cannot be raised in open.
It is an accessory silvicultural system in which selected crops are retained for part or whole of the second rotation to obtain a larger sized timber.

Improvement felling is a method of treatment involving the removal of inferior growing stock with the interest of better growth of more valuable species. It is not considered as a silvicultural system because it is not aimed at regeneration of crop. But this aims at bringing a forest in to a normal state. Improvement felling carried out in the following ways:
Felling of dead, drying and diseased tree
Felling of unsound and over mature tree
Felling of badly shaped mature or immature tree
Thinning of congested groups of poles and trees
Thinning of badly shaped and damaged saplings
Removal of undesirable under growth or tree of inferior species

II) Coppice forest systems Coppice system refers to the silvicultural, system in which the new crop originates mainly from coppice and where the rotation of crop is shorter. different coppice systems are described in detail below

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Simple coppice system
aliases: damaged by wind and animals, rotting possibilities
easy to drain out the rain water

blocks.text: In this fixed area of old crop is clear felled completely without reserving any tree.
Regeneration is obtained through stool coppices.
The coppicing is done little before the start of spring.
Stump height should not be too lower (damaged by wind and animals, rotting possibilities) or too high (causes drying and stump splitting).
Optimum stump height is 15-25 cm.
Cutting of stem should be carried out in a sloppy manner (easy to drain out the rain water) without stripping or splitting the bark (enhance coppicing).
Tending operation is carried out from second years onwards.
Thinning is done according to the management options. Crop obtained is even aged
In this system, at the end of the first rotation of coppice a few selected poles are left over the coupe for the second rotation.
The objective is to obtain a few bigger sized timbers.
In this, selected poles are retained at second rotation onwards and not from initial felling.
In this system, some shelterwoods or standards (125 to 150) are retained at the first clear felling.
The shelter trees should be of most promising ones
These trees are retained till the .coppices established securely.
Thereafter shelter is gradually removed.

The number of standards retained varies with species and conditions. The normal prescribed standards are 125-150/ha at initial. This is reduced to 60-75/ha at 5th year and completely removed at 10th year.

It is a silviculture system based on coppices in which an over wood is of seedling origin and composed of trees of various ages which is kept over coppices for varying periods. The period of retaining standards (over wood) may be multiples of coppice rotation or a permanent one. The main objectives of keeping standards are as follows:
Here the crop is composed of two storeys. Lower storey is of even aged coppices whereas upper storey is made up of different species of different ages. Similarly each storey has specific rotation.

It is a silvicultural system in which felling is done in suitable areas likely to benefit after reserving all financially immature growth of principal as well as other valuable species, either singly or in groups. The trees reserved should be based on economic or protection considerations.
Mature tree - cut and immature tree - not cut
It is a silvicultural system in which fellings are carried out on the principle of selection system but regeneration is obtained through coppice.

Pollarding refers to the cutting off of tree stem usually above the browsing height to obtain a flush of shoots. Pollard system is applicable for obtaining maximum fodder from the tree. Hence this is applicable to Salix spp, Hardwickia binata and mixed dry deciduous forests.

The successfulness of any forestry program is depends on the apt choice of silvicultural systems according to the actual site conditions. The apt choice of silvicultural system considers the following;
Light demanding species: Clear felling system
Shade bearing species: Shelterwood system or selection forest system
Good coppicer: Coppice system
Good seed yielding: High forest system
Species with long seed interval: Selection system
In this system, arable crops are suitably mixed with tree crops. The individual subclasses of the agrisilvicultural systems are described below:

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Improved fallow species in shifting cultivation
aliases: Improved fallow species in shifting cultivation

blocks.text: In this system, planting of trees is done in the fallow, lands at the end of shifting cultivation. This practice decreases soil erosion in the subsequent years and recovers depleted soil nutrients. The species selected should have a capability to restore the nutrient status and reduce erosion.
Additional points:
Fallows are crop land left without crops for periods ranging trom one season to several years.
The objective of improved fallow species in shifting cultivation is to recover depleted soil nutrients. Once the soil has recovered, crops are reintroduced for one or more season.

In taungya system, farmers/local peoples are permitted to raise crops along with tree species in a same land unit. The farmer is responsible for land preparation, tree planting and growing agricultural crops.
Departmental Taungya: In this, agricultural crops and trees are raised by the forest department personals by employing local labourers.
Leased Taungya: In this system, land is given to local peoples on lease for raising crops with in plantation for a specified duration with ensuring tree care.

Village Taungya: In this, crops are raised by the people who have settled down in a village inside the forest. Usually, each family has allotted a land of about 1 to 2 ha to raise trees along with arable crops for 3 to 4 years.
In this system, mixture of various kinds of tree species are grown to provide multiple output such as food,- fodder and wood products,

Alley cropping is also known as hedgerow intercropping. This involves managing rows of woody plants with annual crops in between them. These woody plants are cut regularly so as to facilitate sunlight penetration. These pruned materials are used as mulch. The purpose of alley cropping is to maintain or increase crop yields by improving the soil as well as microclimate. This reduces weeds effectively.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Desired characteristic of the tree for agroforestry system
aliases: Desired characteristic of the tree for agroforestry system

blocks.text: 1) Leguminous trees are preferable as it improves soil fertility. (AFO 2023)
2) The tree should have a sparse, small crown that permits more sunlight.
3) It should resprout rapidly after pruning, coppicing, pollarding or lopping.
4) It should have a deep taproot system with few lateral root branches near the surface,
5) The tree should provide sufficient litter fall.
6) The tree should not have any allelopathic effect.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Multipurpose trees and shrubs on farmland
aliases: Multipurpose trees and shrubs on farmland

blocks.text: In this system, various multipurpose tree species occurs scatterly or in some systematic patterns. This system produces multiple products and offers protective function too. The suitable trees are Leucaena leucocephala, Acacia albida, Cassia siamea, Casuarina equisetifolia, Azadirachta indica, Acacia Senegal, Cocos nucifera etc.
In this, perennial trees and shrub, (coffee, tea, coconut and cocoa) are combined in the intercropping systems.

In this system, fuel wood species are inter-planted on or around agricultural lands. This system acts both fence as well as shelter-belts besides providing fuel wood to local community. Suitable tree species for this system are Acacia nilotica, Albizia lehbek, Cassia siamea, Casuarina equisetifolia, Dalbergiasissoo, Prosopisjuliflora and Eucalyptus tereticornis.

Shelter belts are the belt of rows of trees established at right angles to the prevailing wind direction. Shelterbelt deflects the air currents and thus by reduces the wind velocity and erosion. It provides protection to the leeward areas against wind erosion and decreases the desiccation effects on plants. It also provides food, fodder and timber.

Shelter-belts have a typical pyramidal shape. This is achieved by raising tall trees in centre and medium sized trees in adjacent to both sides. Thereafter, shrubs and grasses are planted in a similar fashion. Shelterbelt up to 50 m width with suitable spacing is ideal. The ratio of the height and width of shelter belt should be roughly 1:10. Shelter-belts are oriented right angled to the prevailing wind direction. Shelter-belts are raised in quadrangles if the wind direction tends to change very often. The minimum length of protection given by a shelter-belt Is about 25 times its height.
The following species are recommended for shelterbelt establishment.
Grasses: Saccharum spontanewn, S. munja, Panicum antidolale and Cencnrus spp.
Shrubs: Calotropis procera, Clerodendronphlomoides, Cassia auriculata, Dodonaia viscosa.

Tree species: Acacia arabica, A. leucopholea, Dalbergia sissoo, Lannea coromandelica, Eucalyptus spp., Tamarix articulata, Parkinsonia aculeata, Prosopis juliflora, Prosopis spicigera, Casuarina equisetifolia.

Windbreak refers to the strip of trees and/or shrubs planted in order to protect fields, homes, canals or other areas from wind and blowing soil. It protects the livestock from cold winds. Shelterbelt protects crops and pastures from hot and drying winds.

It reduces soil erosion and provides habitat for wildlife. It reduces the evaporation from farmlands and improves the microclimate. It acts as a fence and boundary. This retards grass fire during summer season. In addition, windbreak provides useful products such as poles, fuel wood, fruit, fodder, fiber and mulch.

The windbreak should allow portion of wind to pass through. This to reduce’s the wind velocity up to 25 and 75 percent. This acts as a wall and causes uprising of air. This air will fall down after a certain distance. In case of dense windbreaks, air is difficult to permeate the windbreak and causes breakage of trees and considerable turbulence in the downwind side. However, these are useful for areas that require high level of protection and of small extent. The desirable permeability is obtained by selection of trees and providing suitable spacing. Windbreaks are planted at right angles to wind direction. The height of windbreak determines the length of the sheltered area. In the windward side, it protects the area occupying 15 times the tree height from the windbreak whereas in upwind side, it is only 5 times of the tree height.

The length of the windbreaks is effective when it is more than 12 times of the tree height. A single row windbreak is useful for smaller area for which tree species having thick foliage is preferable. If one tree is lost from this row, gap is created, which reduces the efficiency of the entire windbreak. Hence, windbreaks of three to five rows are common in farm conditions. Spacing of tree depends upon the functions of windbreaks. Where the products of wind breaks have a high priority, then land users may favour greater number of shorter strips and a higher proportion of small trees and shrubs which provide products such as fodder and fuel wood. If the by product is timber, the height of wind breaks and the intervals between them can be increased. When the interest is to protect valuable crops, the wind breaks sliould be as tall and as far apart as possible to obtain the more protection. In dry areas, individual plants should be widely spaced so that they do not compete with each other for the available soil moisture.

Gaps are provided wherever gates and tracks required. Wind velocity in these areas is higher due to the funneling effect. This can be managed by providing a gap with a 45 degree angle to the prevailing wind direction. In general, trees with narrow, vertical growth are ideal for windbreak which includes Eucalyptus, Cassia, Prosopis, Leucaena, Casurina, Acacia, Grevillea, Syzygium and Dalbergia species (Rosewood).

10. Soil conservation hedges: In this system, trees can be planted on soil conservation works such as bunds and terraces. These trees augment the conservation work through stabilization of soil. The interception of rain and obstruction of wind reduces the soil erosion. Grevillea robusta. Acacia catechu, Pinus roxburghii. Acacia modesta, Prosopis Juliflora, Alnus nepalensis, and Leucaena are commonly used for this purposes with grasses.

(B) Sllvipasture system Silvipasture refers to the production of woody plants in pasture lands. Here, trees and shrubs mainly provide fodder. The suitable species Acacia hilotica, Albizia lebbeck,. Azadirachta indica, Leucaena leucocephala, Gliricidia sepium and Sesbania grandi/lora.

Live fence of fodder trees and hedges

blocks.text: In this system, fodder trees and hedges are planted along the boundaries which serve as a live fence in addition to providing fodder. The suitable species for this purpose are Guricidia sepium, Seshania grandiflora, Erythrina spp and Acacia species.

In this system, various tree and shrub species are scattered irregularly or arranged systemically which supplements forage production. Acacia nilotica, Acacia leucophloea. Tamahndus indica and Azadirachta indica are used for these purposes.

Agrisilvipastural system refers to the production of woody perennial along with annuals and pastures. This system is grouped into two categories viz., home garden and woody hedgerows for browse, mulch, green manure and soil conservation.

Home gardens are suitable to high rainfall areas in tropical conditions. These are highly productive and sustainable one. Food production is primary function of home gardens. In this system, trees, shrubs, vegetables and other herbaceous plants are grown in dense. These plants are arranged in random both spatially and temporally. Animals also included in many of the home gardens for which fodder grasses and legumes are planted. Homestead occupies an area around 0.20 to 0.50 ha. This system is managed by family labour.

Home garden is also called as Multi-tier system or Multi-tier cropping as it consists of different canopy strata. In this system, herbaceous plant constitutes the ground layer and trees occupy the top storey. In the ground layer, vegetables grown up to one meter height whereas food crops such as banana, papaya occupies layer of 1-3 m. The woody species occupies the top layer which includes Anacardutm occidentale, Artocarpus heterophyllus, Citrus spp., Psidium guajava, Mangifera indica, Azadirachta indica and Cocus nucijera.

In this system, fast growing fodder shrubs and woody hedges are planted for the purpose of mulch, green manure, soil conservation, etc. The suitable species for this system are Erythrina spp, Leucaena luecocephala and Sesbania grandijlora.
1. Apiculture with trees:
In this system, trees producing more flowers and honey are planted with the aim to augments apiculture. (//)

In this system, suitable trees are planted around the fish ponds. The prime objective is to augment the aquaculture by reducing evaporation and augmenting microclimate. Mulberry, salix, Taxoderma, bamboos and eucalyptus are suitable for bank planting surrounding the fish ponds.
In this system, multipurpose trees are grown in a mixed fashion with the objective to provide wood, fodder, soil conservation, soil reclamation, etc.

blocks.text: (a) Crop composition: Crop composition describes the presence of different species in an area along with the proportion of each crop in that area.
(b) Colour: Each forest type or vegetation is given specific colour so as to get a clear idea while reading a stock map.

A) Diameter measurement: In logs, the diameters are measured at thick end, thin end and at the middle of the logs. The average value is considered as a diameter of log. The girth of log is measured in the middle except when stacked. In case of felled trees, the diameter and girth is determined as described above.

In case of standing trees, the diameters or girths can be measured at breast height. Breast height (BH) is defined as the universally adopted standard height for measuring girth, diameters and basal area of standing trees. In India, Burma, America, Union of South Africa and Malaya, it is taken as 1.37 m (4 ft 6 in) above ground level while it is 1.3 m (4 ft 3 in) in Europe, United Kingdom, FAO and other Commonwealth countries.

The most commonly used instruments for diameter or girth measurements are wooden scale, calipers, tape, biltmore stick, sector fork, pentaprism, barr and stround dendrometer, wedge-prism and tele-relaskop.

Wooden scale is a flat wooden piece marked in centimetre and millimetre.
It is available in two sizes, viz., 30 cm and 60 cm.
The 30 cm wooden scale is about 3 cm wide but the 60 cm wooden scale is about 1.5 cm wide and has folding arrangement at every 15 cm length.
Calliper is used to measure the diameter of standing trees and logs.
Callipers are made of wood or alloy. In humid conditions, wood absorbs moisture and the movable arm gets jammed.
Normally callipers exceeding 120 cm in length are rarely used.
The rule is divided into centimetre and millimetre.
In some cases, diameter classes are painted in different colours which helps the usage by illiterate labour for measurement.
Tape is a band of cloth, reinforced cloth, plastic or steel about 1.5 cm wide and of varying length. Tape is used to measure the girth of trees and logs. It is graduated in centimetre and millimetre.

The cloth tapes are painted on both sides to give better look and to protect them from the influence of water. These are cheap and not very durable. These tapes are affected by fluctuations in length due to expansion. This can be avoided by the use of tap reinforced with metal wires. These tapes are called as metallic tapes.
The tapes used in tree measurements are generally 3 m or 5 m in length. The land measuring tapes may be of 5, 10, 20, 30 or 50 m.
Diameter tapes are graduated to read diameter directly by using the relationship between diameter and girth {D - Girth/Pi}.

blocks.text: The thickness of the bark varies with species to species and tree to tree. The bark thickness varies with the age of tree and base to top of the tree. This affects the calculation of volume of standing trees. The thickness of the bark is measured by Swedish bark gauge.

Tree height is one of the components for calculating tree volume. This is required for computing volume ^able, form factor table and yield table. Height of trees indirectly gives the idea about the productive capacity of site or site quality.

Tree height is the straight-line distance from the tip of the leading shoot (highest point of the crown) to the ground level, usually measured on slopes from the uphill side of the tree. The height of a felled tree is measured from the top to the base in a straight line without any allowance for curvature of the stem.
Bole height is the distance between ground level and crown point.
Crown point is the position of the first crown forming living or dead branch. Simply it is the length of the clear main stem of tree.
Commercial bole height is the height of bole that is usually fit for utilization as timber.
Standard timber bole height is the height of the bole from the ground level up to the point where diameter over bark is 20 cm.
Stump is a stem which is left on the ground after felling.
Stump height is the height of the top of the stump above ground.
Crown length is the vertical measurement of the crown of a tree from the tip to the point halfway between the lowest green branches forming green crown.
Crown height is the vertical length from the ground level to the point half way between the lowest green branch and the green branches forming green crown all round.
Crown width is the maximum spread of the crown along its widest diameter. It is the basis of thinning in trees.

Hypsometers, altimeters and clinometers are used in measuring height of trees under different conditions. These instruments are based on geometric principles such as similar triangles principle or trigonometric principles.
1) Brandis hypsometer: Brandis hypsometer consists of a hollow metal tube of about 14 cm long and rectangular cross section. A wheel enclosed in a circular metal case is attached to it on one side.
2) Brandis table: The instrument is provided with a table called brandis table which gives the heights of trees directly.

3) Abney’s level: This is used for measuring height and contouring. It consists of a hollow tube with an eyepiece at one end and a sighting tube at the other end. The spirit level is fitted to the main tube in such a way that one screw or a
wheel. An index arm is attached to the spirit level and the arc is graduated to read whole degrees. A vernier and a magnifying glass are fitted on the index arm.
This instrument is similar to the Abney’s level except for minor differences. The protractor of this instrument is graduated on both sides.
The observer has to stand at one chain distance from the tree and sight the top of the tree.
The reading on the protractor on the side of rise or fall per chain horizontal will give the height of the tree above eye level. By adding observer’s eye height, the height of the tree is obtained.
In this, tree height is given readily without reference to mathematical tables.
It is fairly simple to use. But the height obtained is of approximate value only. This is difficult to use in forest.
It consists of a pointer and a rotatable scale. The top of the case has an eye piece with a pinhole.
The instrument has hexagonal bar inside which can be rotated by a turning knob.
The bar has a separate scale on each of its face. The usual height scales are 15, 20, 25 and 30.

In order to use this instrument, the observer should stand at specific distance (15, 20,25 or 30 m) by holding the instrument in such a way that the eye piece is towards the observer and the sight vane is towards the tree.
6) Relaskop: The Spiegel relaskop is used for measurement of basal area of crops, diameters over bark at any distance from the tree.
Christen hypsometer is designed based on similar triangle principle.
This instrument consists of a rule or scale of about 10 inches long.
For measuring tree height, a 10-foot pole is placed upright at the base of the tree.
Then the forester stands at sufficient distance from tree in such a way that the two inside edges of the flanges are in line with the top and base of the tree.

Stacked volume is not the actual volume of solid volume of fuel stacks. The value of fuel is based on the solid content. The solid volume of firewood depends upon the factors such as stacking, form of billets, length and diameter of the billets. The solid volume can be assessed by any one of following ways:

1) Xylometric method: Xylometer is a graduated vessel and volume of wood is calculated by the principle of water displacement. The wood pieces are submerged in the water in the vessel. The volume increment in the vessel gives the actual solid volume of wood. As the stack volume is huge, a sample portion is utilized and the results extrapolated for the whole log using the formulae given below:
This method is cumbersome and seldom used in practice.
2) Specific gravity method: The fuel wood weight is calculated by using the relationship between the specific gravity and volume of wood.

Mixing seed with sand or ash facilitates broadcasting the seed. The bed should be watered regularly. The seed germinates in about 3-5 weeks.

Dibbling implies planting in holes. The bits of mown grasses are used for dibbling. The cutting with inter nodes is used for dibbling. Dibbling of grass is done at a distance of 10 cm in the moist bed. The dibbled grasses start growth in about 5-6 weeks.

Carbon dioxide (CO2) in the air is the primary source of the elemental carbon. The photosynthetic process in plants fixes the atmospheric CO2 as various plant biomasses. The decomposition of biomass results in the release of CO2 back into atmosphere.

The combustion of fossil fuels (oil and gasoline) increases the concentration of CO2 in atmosphere. Carbon dioxide plays a role in absorbing radiated heat and in regulating global atmospheric temperatures. A rise in CO2 levels in the atmosphere will tend to increases the average temperature.

The nitrogen cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that describes the transformations of nitrogen and nitrogen-containing compounds in nature. Earth’s atmosphere contains about 78% nitrogen, making it the largest pool of nitrogen. Nitrogen is essential for many biological processes. The various steps in N cycles is given below:

Nitrogen fixation: Biological nitrogen fixation refers to the conversion of N2 from the atmospheric nitrogen into a living biomass (biological). Nitrogen fixation in soil may be of biological fixation (BGA, Azotobacter, rhizobium) or industrial fixation (ammonia production) or physical fixation by lightning.

Assimilation: It refers the uptake of available N by the plants and microbes. Simply it is the conversion or fixation of inorganic nitrogen into organic forms in living biomass. This organic form of N is added to the soil in the form of organic residues of living organisms.
Ammonification: It refers the conversion of organic nitrogen (biomass) into inorganic nitrogen through decomposition by microbes. This is a part of mineralization process.

Nitrification: It is the conversion of ammonia to nitrates in soil. This is carried out by the soil living bacteria and other nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas (converts ammonia to nitrites NO2) and Nitrobacter (converts N02 into NO3). This is readily available to plants and hence plants take this and accumulate in its biomass. This is again recycled to soil by the addition of leaf litter and the above processes are repeated.

Denitrification: It is the reduction of nitrites into nitrogen gas (N2). This process is performed by Pseudomonas and Clostridium under anaerobic conditions. Thus N is again released back to the atmosphere and recycled.

concepts.subject: Forestry
concepts.title: Genetic drift, Hardy Weinberg law significance
aliases: Genetic drift, Hardy Weinberg law significance

blocks.text: It is also called as genetic sampling error or Sewall Wright effect. Genetic drift or allelic drift is the change in the frequency of a gene variant (allele) in a population due to random sampling. In general when the population is large, the effect of genetic drift is very less. If population is small, sampling error alter the allele frequency. Genetic drift is considered as a mechanism of evolutionary change within small populations.

It is also recognized as the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, model, theorem, or law. It states that allele and genotype frequencies in a population will remain constant from generation to generation in the absence of other evolutionary influences such as include mate choice, mutation, selection, genetic drift, gene flow and meiotic drive.

In natural population, always one or more of these evolutionary influences typically presence and hence this principle is not applicable for natural population. Hardy-Weinberg principle explains the ideal condition against. This ideal population can be used for checking or analysing the other influences on the genotypic frequency change.

This law proves that natural selection is vital for evolutionary process. Hardy-Weinberg Law allow the variability (the existence of differentalleles) and inheritance, but they eliminate natural selection.

Hardy-Weinberg Law helps to appraise the effect of selection pressures by measuring the difference between ideal, actual and ideal allelic frequencies or phenotypes. In order to obtain ideal allele frequency, Hardy-Weinberg equation is needed. This aids to hypothesize the population’s evolution.

blocks.text: Shade net house aids growing seedlings under reduced sunlight condition. This is vital during the initial stage of seedlings, cuttings and graftage. Owing to reduced sunlight, moisture loss is minimized from seedlings which ensures success of sprouting from cuttings and graftage. Further, it ensures protection of seedlings from pest and diseases.

Desired dimension of shade net nursery (e.g., 20 x 10 x 2 m) is to be erected using GI pipes as main support. Wired grid is provided at the top of GI pipe structure. The entire structure is covered with shade nets. Shade nets are black in colour and available with varying permissible light intensity. UV stabilized HDPE shade net with 50 per cent shade intensity is useful for nursery. Provision for ventilation is to be given to regulate aeration and temperature inside the shade net nursery.

Similar to tunnels, poly-tunnels are the low height tunnels made up of steel frames covered with poly ethylene/plastic films/plastic nets. It is also referred as hoop greenhouse, hoop house, grow tunnel or high tunnel.

The height of the structure is up to 1 m. It usually covers few rows of crops both in field or in nursery. The purpose of poly-tunnel is to provide protection to the plants against frost, winds and insect/ pest.

The interior of tunnels heats up owing to incoming solar radiation and hence it is most useful to temperate regions. The inside growing condition can be modified either through manual opening and closing or through installing climate control machines (heating, cooling, moisture supply, etc.)

Mist chamber is a specialized propagation structure which is provided with mist system. Similar to green house, it is made up of metal frame and covered with polyethylene sheets. The foggers produce mist inside the mist chamber.

This is widely used for rooting of soft wood, semi hardwood, hardwood and herbaceous cuttings. Mist produced reduces the water loss from cuttings by reducing air temperature and raises relative humidity. After running foggers every time, it is vital to run the fan for few minutes to evaporate the water condensed on the cuttings. This avoids rotting of cuttings and avoids fungal infections.

These are the small beds made up of manures and soil and covered with polyethylene sheets using steel frames. Trench of 50 cm depth, 100 cm width and desired lengths are to be made. At the base straw litter is placed to a thickness of three inch and above which manure is spread for 3 inches thickness. Again straw/liter is placed to a thickness of 3 inch over which dug out soil is placed for about 3 inch thick. Fine fertile soil placed over this on which seeds are sown.

The entire bed is covered with a bottomless box. This box is covered with transparent plastic film either on the top or both top and all sides. Top portion is made like a lid. The height of this box is up to 3 feet as similar to low tunnels. Provision of artificial heat source is also given such as electric cable to increase the temperature inside the hot beds.

The bed heated up by the incoming solar energy. Heat energy is produced inside the hot beds through the decomposition of straw/leaf litter/compost. Further, the heat escape is reduced by the plastic films. Owing to these reasons, temperature of the heat bed is higher (3-10°C) than the outside temperature.

Now a day, wooden frames or brick structures are available on the top covered with transparent glass or polyethylene sheets. This is widely used in temperate condition for small scale vegetable production. As temperature is higher, it is possible to grow seedlings in the cold season as well as off seasons. It protects the seedling from adverse cold conditions.
Manure releases heat only for two months and hence it is vital to shift hot beds every 2-3 months if artificial heat source is not provided.
